title: The Indus Cities
description: An illustrated map of the Indus civilisation, from the first farmers at Mehrgarh through the planned cities of Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira and their trade with Mesopotamia, to their decline and rediscovery.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Indus civilisation, from about 7000 BCE to its rediscovery
note: Based on excavated sites and on Mesopotamian texts; each chapter says which it follows. The Indus script is undeciphered, so no ruler, city or person of the civilisation is known by their own name, and the names used are modern ones. Dates are approximate and many are debated. The map is stylised and not to scale, and the extent under Extent is painted loosely. Rivers are drawn on their courses today; several ran differently then, and the Ghaggar-Hakra is not drawn.

steps.title: First farmers at Mehrgarh
steps.text: At the foot of the Bolan Pass, villagers at Mehrgarh grow wheat and barley and herd cattle, sheep and goats from about 7000 BCE, among the earliest farmers in South Asia. They build mud-brick houses and bury their dead with ornaments; some teeth even show holes drilled by early dentists. Dates for the first layers are debated.
steps.today: Today: near Sibi, Balochistan, Pakistan.

steps.title: Early towns
steps.text: Over thousands of years, farming villages spread across the Indus plains. Harappa’s first settlement dates to about 3300 BCE, and marks scratched on some of its pots may be early forms of the later script. Towns such as Kot Diji in Sindh build walls, and pottery styles grow alike across a wide region.
steps.today: Today: Harappa, Sahiwal district, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: A ploughed field
steps.text: At Kalibangan, beside the dry bed of the Ghaggar river, archaeologists found a field ploughed in a criss-cross pattern, sealed beneath the later town: one of the oldest ploughed fields known. Local farmers still sow two crops together in the same pattern. The later town has a walled citadel and a row of fire altars.
steps.today: Today: Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan, India.

steps.title: A planned city
steps.text: Around 2600 BCE, cities rise across the Indus region. Mohenjo-daro, beside the Indus, is one of the largest: a raised citadel and a lower town of straight streets, baked-brick houses, hundreds of wells and covered drains. Bricks across the civilisation share one shape, 1 by 2 by 4. Its population is unknown; estimates of tens of thousands are disputed.
steps.today: Today: Larkana district, Sindh, Pakistan; a World Heritage Site since 1980.

steps.title: The Great Bath
steps.text: On the citadel lies the Great Bath, a brick tank about 12 by 7 metres and over 2 metres deep, with steps at each end, sealed with gypsum mortar and a layer of bitumen. Its purpose is unknown; many scholars think it was for ritual bathing. A large building nearby is often called the granary, though its use is debated.
steps.today: Today: The Great Bath can still be seen at Mohenjo-daro.

steps.title: The city that named a civilisation
steps.text: Harappa, on an old course of the Ravi, grows into a city of walled mounds with gateways, workshops and a cemetery. It was the first city excavated, so archaeologists call the whole civilisation Harappan. Here, as elsewhere, no palace, royal tomb or ruler’s statue has been found, and how the cities were governed is unknown.
steps.today: Today: Harappa, Sahiwal district, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: A city of reservoirs
steps.text: On Khadir island in the salt flats of the Rann of Kutch, Dholavira catches water from seasonal streams in a chain of large reservoirs cut into rock. Its citadel, middle town and lower town sit inside stone walls. Near the north gate lay a signboard of ten large signs, once inlaid in white gypsum, one of the longest Indus inscriptions.
steps.today: Today: Kutch district, Gujarat, India; a World Heritage Site since 2021.

steps.title: Rakhigarhi and the lost river
steps.text: Rakhigarhi, in the plain of the Ghaggar-Hakra river, is among the largest Indus sites. Hundreds of settlements once lined this river, which today flows only in the monsoon. Some identify it with the Sarasvati of the Rigveda; that link is debated. A 2019 DNA study of a woman buried here found no ancestry from the Central Asian steppe.
steps.today: Today: Hisar district, Haryana, India.

steps.title: Seals and an unread script
steps.text: Thousands of small square seals, mostly of carved stone (steatite), show an animal, often a one-horned bull, beneath a line of signs. Traders probably pressed them into clay to mark goods. The script has about 400 signs, and most inscriptions are very short. It has never been deciphered, so the language and the names of its writers are unknown.
steps.today: Today: Indus seals are in museums in Pakistan, India and beyond.

steps.title: The Dancing Girl and the Priest-King
steps.text: Mohenjo-daro’s best-known finds are small. A bronze figure of a young woman, about 10 centimetres tall, was nicknamed the Dancing Girl by its excavators. A bearded man in a patterned robe, carved in stone, was nicknamed the Priest-King, though nothing shows that he was either. Who they were is not known.
steps.today: Today: The Dancing Girl is in the National Museum, New Delhi; the Priest-King in the National Museum of Pakistan, Karachi.

steps.title: Beads, shell and metal
steps.text: Indus craftworkers are famous for long beads of red carnelian, drilled lengthwise with fine stone drills, slow work that could take days for one bead. Lothal, near carnelian sources on the Gulf of Khambhat, has a bead workshop; Chanhudaro in Sindh is another craft town. Workshops also cut shell bangles and cast copper and bronze tools.
steps.today: Today: Ahmedabad district, Gujarat, India.

steps.title: Lapis from the mountains
steps.text: Far to the north, on the Amu Darya (Oxus) in today’s Afghanistan, Shortughai is an Indus outpost with Harappan pottery, bricks and a seal. It lies near the mountains of Badakhshan, the main ancient source of blue lapis lazuli. Lapis probably travelled from here to the Indus cities, and on to Mesopotamia.
steps.today: Today: Takhar province, Afghanistan.

steps.title: The dock at Lothal
steps.text: At Lothal, a brick-lined basin over 200 metres long was identified by its excavator, S. R. Rao, as a dock for boats coming in from the gulf. Others argue it was a reservoir for fresh water. A round seal of a kind made in the Persian Gulf, found here, shows that Lothal’s trade did reach overseas.
steps.today: Today: Ahmedabad district, Gujarat, India.

steps.title: Ships from Meluhha
steps.text: Mesopotamian texts name a distant land, Meluhha, most likely the Indus region. Around 2300 BCE King Sargon of Akkad boasts that ships from Meluhha, Magan (Oman) and Dilmun (Bahrain) moor at his capital. Indus seals and carnelian beads turn up at Ur and other Mesopotamian cities. Walled coastal posts such as Sutkagen Dor lie on the route west.
steps.today: Today: Sutkagen Dor is near Jiwani, Balochistan, Pakistan; Mesopotamia is in Iraq.

steps.title: The cities empty
steps.text: After about 1900 BCE the great cities shrink and are slowly abandoned, and the seals, script and standard weights fall out of use. Why is debated: weaker monsoon rains, rivers changing course, the Ghaggar-Hakra drying and less trade with Mesopotamia are all suggested. There is no sign of a single disaster. Kalibangan is abandoned around this time.
steps.today: Today: Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan, India.

steps.title: Moving east and south
steps.text: The people do not vanish. Villages of the later, simpler Harappan phase grow in number east into Haryana and the Ganga–Yamuna plain, where Alamgirpur near Meerut is the easternmost site, and south through Gujarat. Daimabad, on the Pravara river in Maharashtra, is the southernmost; a hoard of bronze figures found there is of debated date.
steps.today: Today: Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, India.

steps.title: Ruins and railway bricks
steps.text: In the late 1820s the traveller Charles Masson describes a ruined brick fortress at Harappa. Alexander Cunningham of the Archaeological Survey visits in the 1850s and 1870s, but railway builders have by then carted away many of its bricks as track ballast. In 1875 he publishes a seal with unknown signs, which he thinks is foreign.
steps.today: Today: Harappa’s mounds are a protected site with a museum.

steps.title: A civilisation announced
steps.text: In 1921 Daya Ram Sahni begins digging at Harappa. In 1922 R. D. Banerji, studying a Buddhist stupa at Mohenjo-daro, finds far older layers beneath it. Seals from the two sites, about 600 kilometres apart, match. In 1924 John Marshall, head of the Archaeological Survey, announces a forgotten civilisation in the Illustrated London News.
steps.today: Today: The stupa still stands on top of Mohenjo-daro’s citadel.

steps.title: The invasion that wasn’t
steps.text: In the 1940s Mortimer Wheeler argues that invaders destroyed the cities, pointing to skeletons in Mohenjo-daro’s streets and the war god Indra of the Rigveda. Later study showed the skeletons come from different periods, with no signs of a battle. Most archaeologists now reject an invasion, though how Indo-European languages reached India is still debated.
steps.today: Today: Mohenjo-daro’s brick ruins are threatened by salt and floods.

steps.title: Still unread
steps.text: Excavated by R. S. Bisht from 1990, Dholavira became a World Heritage Site in 2021, joining Mohenjo-daro. Over a thousand Indus sites are now known, across an area larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia together. Yet the script is still unread. Until it is, the people of the Indus cities speak only through what they built and left behind.
steps.today: Today: Kutch district, Gujarat, India.

items.name: Indus civilisation

facts.Largest cities: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala and Dholavira
facts.Today: Pakistan, north-west India and north-east Afghanistan

rulers.text: Not named: no ruler’s name survives

items.role: One of the world’s first urban civilisations, alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia, spread along the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra.

ties.text: An outpost at Shortughai, near the lapis mines of Badakhshan
Trades by sea with Magan, Dilmun and Mesopotamia, which most likely knows it as Meluhha

items.name: Jean-François Jarrige
items.text: Jarrige led the French team that, with Catherine Jarrige and Pakistani colleagues, excavated Mehrgarh from 1974. Their work pushed the story of the Indus civilisation back by thousands of years, showing a long run of farming villages in the region before the cities.

items.name: B. B. Lal
items.text: Braj Basi Lal, later Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, excavated Kalibangan with B. K. Thapar in the 1960s, uncovering the ploughed field and the fire altars. He also dug at places linked with the epics, and some of his later views are debated.

items.name: R. S. Bisht
items.text: Ravindra Singh Bisht led the Archaeological Survey’s excavation of Dholavira from 1990, uncovering its reservoirs, its three-part plan and the great signboard. Earlier he excavated Banawali in Haryana. His work laid the ground for Dholavira’s listing as a World Heritage Site in 2021.

items.name: S. R. Rao
items.text: Shikaripura Ranganatha Rao excavated Lothal from 1955 to 1960 and identified its great basin as a dock. He later turned to underwater archaeology off Dwarka. His claim to have read the Indus script as an early form of Sanskrit is not accepted by most scholars.

items.name: Charles Masson
items.text: Born James Lewis in London, he deserted the East India Company’s army and travelled under a new name through the Punjab and Afghanistan, collecting tens of thousands of coins. His account, published in 1842, gives the first known description of an Indus city, Harappa.

items.name: Alexander Cunningham
items.role: First head of the Archaeological Survey of India
items.text: A British army engineer, Cunningham became the first head of the Archaeological Survey in 1861 and traced many Buddhist sites using the account of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang. He visited Harappa but could not place the seal he found there; its real age was recognised about fifty years later.

items.name: Daya Ram Sahni
items.text: Sahni began the first full excavation of Harappa in 1921. He later became the first Indian Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, from 1931 to 1935.

items.name: R. D. Banerji
items.text: Rakhal Das Banerji went to Mohenjo-daro in 1922 to study a Buddhist stupa and found seals and remains far older beneath it. He was also a historian and a novelist in Bengali. His share of the credit for the discovery was long overlooked.

items.name: John Marshall
items.role: Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, 1902 to 1928
items.text: Marshall saw that the finds from Harappa and Mohenjo-daro belonged together and announced them in 1924 as a civilisation as old as Sumer. He also led long excavations at Taxila and Sanchi. He suggested that a figure on one seal was an early form of Shiva, an idea still debated.

items.name: Mortimer Wheeler
items.role: Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, 1944 to 1948
items.text: A British archaeologist and soldier, Wheeler dug at Harappa in 1946 and trained a generation of South Asian archaeologists in careful excavation. His vivid claim that the war god Indra ‘stands accused’ of destroying the cities made headlines, but later work rejected it.
